91: Hill reiterates that the lack of understanding about emotionalizing thoughts is the main reason most people who try autosuggestion get no results. Plain, unemotional words do not influence the subconscious—one must reach it with thoughts or spoken words well emotionalized with BELIEF. He warns against discouragement if emotions can't be controlled initially, reminding readers there is no SOMETHING FOR NOTHING. The price of influencing the subconscious is everlasting PERSISTENCE in applying the principles. Wisdom and cleverness alone won't attract money except in rare cases where the law of averages favors it—but this method doesn't depend on the law of averages, plays no favorites, and works equally for all. Where failure occurs, it is the individual, not the method, that failed. The ability to use autosuggestion depends largely on capacity to CONCENTRATE on a given DESIRE until it becomes a BURNING OBSESSION. Hill then offers suggestions for effective concentration: when carrying out the first action step (fixing the exact amount of money), hold thoughts on that amount with eyes closed until you can ACTUALLY SEE the physical appearance of the money, doing this at least once daily.
92: Hill instructs readers to follow Chapter 2's FAITH instructions and see themselves actually IN POSSESSION OF THE MONEY during concentration exercises. He explains the subconscious takes any orders given in absolute FAITH and acts upon them, though orders often need repetition before being interpreted. He suggests playing a 'perfectly legitimate trick' on the subconscious by making it believe, because you believe it, that you must have the money, that it's already awaiting your claim, and that the subconscious MUST hand over practical plans for acquiring it. Hand over this thought to IMAGINATION and see what it creates. DO NOT WAIT for a definite plan—begin at once seeing yourself in possession, DEMANDING and EXPECTING that the subconscious will provide plans. When plans appear (probably through the sixth sense as inspiration), put them into ACTION IMMEDIATELY. Treat inspiration as a direct 'telegram' from Infinite Intelligence—failure to act is FATAL to success. He warns against trusting reason when creating plans—reason is faulty and may be lazy. When visualizing the money, see yourself rendering the service or delivering the merchandise intended in return—this is important.
93: Under 'Summary of Instructions,' Hill states that reading this book indicates earnest seeking of knowledge, but learning requires humility. If one follows some instructions but neglects others—failure is certain. ALL instructions must be followed in a spirit of FAITH. He summarizes and blends the six action steps with autosuggestion principles. First: go to a quiet spot (preferably in bed at night), close eyes, and repeat aloud the written statement of the amount of money, time limit, and service or merchandise to give in return. SEE YOURSELF ALREADY IN POSSESSION OF THE MONEY. He provides a detailed example statement: 'By the first day of January, [year], I will have in my possession $500,000, which will come to me in various amounts from time to time during the interim. In return for this money I will give the most efficient service of which I am capable...I believe that I will have this money in my possession. My faith is so strong that I can now see this money before...'
94: The example statement continues: '...my eyes. I can touch it with my hands. It is now awaiting transfer to me at the time and in the proportion that I deliver the service I intend to render in return for it. I am awaiting a plan by which to accumulate this money, and I will follow that plan when it is received.' Second: repeat this program night and morning until you can clearly visualize the money. Third: place a written copy where you can see it night and morning, reading it before retiring and upon arising until memorized. Hill reminds readers they are applying the Law of Autosuggestion to give orders to the subconscious. These instructions apply to any desire or goal, not just money. The subconscious acts ONLY upon instructions emotionalized with feeling—FAITH is the strongest and most productive emotion. He acknowledges the instructions may seem abstract but urges following them regardless. Skepticism is characteristic of all humans with new ideas, but following the instructions replaces skepticism with belief, then ABSOLUTE FAITH, reaching the point where one can truly say: 'I am the Master of my Fate, I am the Captain of my Soul!'
95: Hill explains that philosophers have stated each person is master of their earthly destiny but failed to say why. This chapter explains why: we have the POWER TO INFLUENCE OUR OWN SUBCONSCIOUS MIND, and through it, to gain the cooperation of Infinite Intelligence. He calls this chapter the 'keystone in the arch of The Think and Grow Rich Philosophy'—its instructions must be understood and APPLIED WITH PERSISTENCE. The other principles are simply tools for applying autosuggestion. He urges readers to carry out instructions with the FAITH of a child, noting he has carefully included no impractical instructions. After reading the entire book, readers should return to this chapter and: READ THE ENTIRE CHAPTER ALOUD ONCE EVERY NIGHT until thoroughly convinced autosuggestion is sound and will accomplish all claimed. AS YOU READ, UNDERSCORE WITH A PENCIL every sentence that impresses you favorably. Following these instructions opens the way for mastery of all success principles, including the next: SPECIALIZED KNOWLEDGE, The Fourth Step to Riches.
96: This page features a single inspirational quote in large text: 'I BELIEVE THAT CLOSE ASSOCIATION WITH ONE WHO REFUSES TO COMPROMISE WITH CIRCUMSTANCES HE OR SHE DOES NOT LIKE IS AN ASSET THAT CAN NEVER BE MEASURED IN TERMS OF MONEY.' This quote, attributed to Napoleon Hill, serves as a thematic epigraph introducing Chapter 4 on Specialized Knowledge. It encapsulates the principle that surrounding oneself with determined, uncompromising individuals is an immeasurable advantage—a concept that connects to the Master Mind principle discussed later in the book. The page functions as a motivational divider between chapters.
97: This page opens Chapter 4: SPECIALIZED KNOWLEDGE—Personal Experiences or Observations (The Fourth Step to Riches). Hill distinguishes two kinds of knowledge: general and specialized. General knowledge, however great in quantity or variety, is of little use in accumulating money. University faculties possess practically every form of general knowledge, yet most professors haven't amassed great wealth—they specialize in teaching but not in organizing or using knowledge for money accumulation. KNOWLEDGE will not attract money unless organized and intelligently directed through practical PLANS OF ACTION to the DEFINITE END of accumulating money. The belief that 'knowledge is power' is false—knowledge is only potential power, becoming power only when organized into definite plans directed to a definite end. The 'missing link' in all education systems is the failure to teach students HOW TO ORGANIZE AND USE KNOWLEDGE AFTER ACQUIRING IT. Many assume Henry Ford was uneducated due to little schooling, but they don't know Ford or understand the real meaning of 'educate.'
98: Hill traces the word 'educate' to the Latin 'educo,' meaning to educe, draw out, DEVELOP FROM WITHIN. An educated person is not necessarily one with abundant knowledge but one who has developed mental faculties sufficiently to acquire anything desired without violating others' rights—Ford fits this definition. During WWI, a Chicago newspaper called Ford 'an ignorant pacifist.' Ford sued for libel. The paper's attorneys put Ford on the witness stand to prove his ignorance, asking questions like 'Who was Benedict Arnold?' and 'How many soldiers did the British send to put down the Rebellion of 1776?' Ford replied to the latter: 'I do not know the exact number...but I have heard that it was a considerably larger number than ever went back.' Finally tiring of offensive questions, Ford leaned over, pointed at the lawyer, and said: 'If I should really WANT to answer your foolish questions...let me remind you that I have a row of electric push-buttons on my desk, and by pushing the right button, I can summon to my aid men who can answer ANY question I desire to ask concerning the business to which I am devoting most of my efforts. Now, will you kindly tell me WHY I should clutter up my mind with general knowledge...when I have men around me who can supply any knowledge I require?' The reply floored the lawyer—everyone recognized it as the answer of an educated man.
99: Hill states that anyone who knows where to get knowledge when needed and how to organize it into definite plans is educated. Through his Master Mind Group, Ford had all specialized knowledge needed to become one of America's wealthiest individuals—it wasn't essential to have it in his own mind. Before transmuting DESIRE into monetary equivalent, one requires SPECIALIZED KNOWLEDGE of the service, merchandise, or profession to offer in return. If one needs more knowledge than one can acquire, one can bridge the weakness through a Master Mind Group. Andrew Carnegie stated he knew nothing about the technical end of steel and didn't care to—he found specialized knowledge through his Master Mind Group's individual units. Great fortunes require POWER, acquired through highly organized and intelligently directed specialized knowledge, but that knowledge doesn't need to be in the fortune accumulator's possession. This should encourage those with ambition but limited education. The person who can organize and direct a Master Mind Group possessing useful knowledge is as educated as anyone in the group. Edison had only three months of formal education yet didn't lack education or die poor. Ford had less than sixth-grade schooling but did pretty well financially.
100: Hill declares SPECIALIZED KNOWLEDGE is among the most plentiful and cheapest forms of service available—consult any college payroll for proof. Under 'It Pays to Know How to Purchase Knowledge,' he advises: first decide the sort of specialized knowledge needed and its purpose. The major purpose in life helps determine what knowledge is needed. Then find accurate information about dependable sources: (a) one's own experience and education, (b) experience and education through cooperation of others (Master Mind Alliance), (c) colleges and universities, (d) public libraries (books and periodicals containing all knowledge organized by civilization), and (e) special training courses (night schools and home study). Knowledge must be organized and put to use for a definite purpose through practical plans—it has no value except through application toward some worthy end. This is why a college degree alone isn't valued more highly—it often represents nothing but miscellaneous knowledge. If pursuing additional formal education, first determine the purpose, then find where that specific knowledge can be obtained. Successful people never stop acquiring specialized knowledge related to their major purpose. Those who are unsuccessful usually believe the 'knowledge-acquiring' period ends when school finishes. The truth is formal education merely puts one in the way of learning how to acquire practical knowledge.
